extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of poetics/literary composition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and judging poetic works (especially tragedy and epic): covers diction (word-types, metaphor, licenses), plot unity and structure, metre choice, characterization, and the use of the wonderful and plausibility. Emphasises balance, moderation, and genre-appropriate choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence / Phrase unity
rubrics_metrics.description: A Sentence or Phrase is a composite significant sound, some at least of whose parts are in themselves significant. A sentence or phrase may form a unity in two ways—either as signifying one thing, or as consisting of several parts linked together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the definition of man' is unified by the thing signified; the Iliad is unified by linking together of parts. A sentence may even dispense with the verb and still be a unity (e.g., 'in walking', 'Cleon son of Cleon'). Use this principle when constructing coherent expressions or syntactic units in poetry and prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb as marker of time and inflection
rubrics_metrics.description: A Verb is a composite significant sound, marking time, in which, as in the noun, no part is in itself significant. Inflexion belongs both to the noun and verb, and expresses relations (e.g., 'of', 'to') or number (singular/plural) or modes/tones (question/command).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that verbal forms carry temporal and modal information essential to meaning; choose inflections deliberately to convey tense, relation, and mode. Examples given: 'Did he go?' vs 'go' as verbal inflections; use of inflection affects how action and relation are perceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of words (simple/double/multiple; current/strange/metaphorical/ornamental/newly-coined/lengthened/contracted/altered)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words are simple (composed of non-significant elements) or double/compound (composed of a significant and non-significant element or multiple significant elements). Every word is either current, or strange, or metaphorical, or ornamental, or newly-coined, or lengthened, or contracted, or altered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions and diagnostic examples: 'current' = in general use among a people; 'strange' = current in another country; 'metaphorical' = transference of name; 'newly-coined' = invented by the poet; 'lengthened' = vowel exchanged/ syllable inserted; 'contracted' = part removed; 'altered' = part retained and part recast. Use these categories to judge diction, tone, and appropriateness for genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of metaphor (genus↔species, species↔species) and analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor is the application of an alien name by transference either from genus to species, from species to genus, from species to species, or by analogy/proportion (the second term is to the first as the fourth to the third).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: genus→species ('There lies my ship'—lying at anchor is a species of lying); species→genus ('ten thousand' as large number); species→species ('to draw away' used for 'to cleave'). You may qualify metaphors by adding the term to which the proper word is relative ('the shield of Dionysus'). Metaphors can be used even when a specific word does not exist for a term (use proportional analogy, e.g., 'sowing the god-created light').

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy/proportion as source of metaphorical expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy or proportion is when the second term is to the first as the fourth is to the third; one may use the fourth for the second or the second for the fourth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogical substitutions to create striking metaphors (e.g., cup: Dionysus :: shield:Ares → 'shield of Dionysus'). Proportional metaphors can name relations for which no existing term exists; exercise care to preserve clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of style: clear without being mean
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of style is to be clear without being mean. The clearest style is that which uses only current or proper words; at the same time purely current diction tends to be mean, while unusual words raise diction above common-place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a balance: proper/current words provide perspicuity; strange/rare/metaphorical/ornamental words provide loftiness. A style wholly of metaphors becomes a riddle; wholly of rare words becomes a jargon. An infusion of unusual elements is necessary but must be moderated to avoid obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and moderation in use of licenses (metaphor, rare words, lengthening/etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of lengthening, contraction, alteration, metaphors, strange or rare words, and other similar licenses must be moderate; employed obtrusively they are grotesque or ludicrous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: excessive or obtrusive licenses produce caricature (Eucleides' caricature of lengthening syllables). Even metaphors and rare words used without propriety for the sake of effect will make diction ludicrous. Use licenses sparingly and where they improve distinction without sacrificing intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lengthening, contraction, and alteration as tools for distinction without sacrificing clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Lengthening, contraction, and alteration of words contribute to clearness of diction remote from commonness and give distinction while partial conformity with usage gives perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deviate from the normal idiom in exceptional cases to gain distinction; critics who universally censure such licenses are in error. Use these devices where they produce rhetorical effect and maintain reader/listener comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of metaphor as highest poetic skill
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest thing by far is to have a command of metaphor. This alone cannot be imparted by another; it is the mark of genius, for to make good metaphors implies an eye for resemblances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a sensitivity to likenesses and analogies; good metaphors are central to elevated diction and are especially valued in certain genres. This skill is a distinctive criterion of excellence in poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriate diction (mapping word-types to genres)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different kinds of words are best adapted to different poetic forms: compound words suit dithyrambs; rare words suit heroic poetry; metaphors suit iambic; in heroic poetry all varieties are serviceable; iambic, which reproduces familiar speech, should use words found in prose (current/proper, metaphorical, ornamental).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose diction according to metre and genre: heroic verse tolerates and benefits from rare words and metaphors; iambic aims to mimic colloquial speech and thus favors current/proper vocabulary. Match word-types to expected genre conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot unity for narrative imitation (single action with beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: For poetic imitation narrative in single metre, the plot ought to be constructed on dramatic principles: it should have as its subject a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end—resembling a single and coherent organism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to cover an entire vast subject if it cannot be embraced in a single view; detach a single portion and admit episodes where appropriate (as Homer does). Distinguish poetic plots from historical compositions, which present a single period rather than a single action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and manageable scope (beginning and end within single view)
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning and the end must be capable of being brought within a single view; poems should be of a scale answering to the group of tragedies presented at a single sitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit scope to what can be grasped as a coherent whole. Epic may enlarge its dimensions compared with tragedy, but still should keep the action or the subject within a viewable, manageable scope to preserve unity and integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic requires the same parts as Tragedy (reversals, recognitions, incidents); diction and thought must be artistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry must have as many kinds as Tragedy and (except for song and spectacle) requires the same parts—Reversals of the Situation, Recognitions, and Tragic Incidents; the thoughts and diction must be artistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing epic, include structural elements associated with tragic plot where appropriate; ensure that thought and diction rise to artistic standards, using Homer as the exemplar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of simultaneous events in epic for mass and variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry, owing to its narrative form, can present many events simultaneously transacted; if relevant to the subject, these add mass and dignity to the poem and relieve sameness of incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit the narrative form to introduce simultaneous or parallel actions that enrich the poem's scale and variety, but ensure relevance and avoid producing satiety on repeated similar incidents (which makes stage tragedies fail).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and propriety of metre (heroic measure favored for epic; don't mix metres)
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroic measure is the stateliest and most massive; it most readily admits rare words and metaphors. The iambic and trochaic tetrameter are stirring measures—the trochaic akin to dancing, the iambic expressive of action. Mixing different metres is incongruous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose metre appropriate to scale and tone: heroic for large narrative epic and to admit elevated diction; iambic/trochaic for action and performance. Avoid mixing metres within a large-scale narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's persona: minimal authorial intrusion and strong characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak as little as possible in his own person; the imitator's role is not to appear but to present characters. Each personage brought in should possess characteristic qualities—each with a character of his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit authorial commentary; let characters speak and act to convey their nature. Introduce characters quickly and distinctly so they are recognisable by characteristic traits (Homer as model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admittance of the wonderful but preference for probable plausibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of the wonderful is admitted in Tragedy and has wider scope in Epic (the irrational can be presented more easily in narrative), and the wonderful is pleasing. Nevertheless, the poet should prefer probable possibilities to improbable ones; the tragic plot must not be composed of irrational parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extraordinary or 'wonderful' elements to please and surprise, but keep them anchored in plausibility where possible. Avoid constructing plots made up of irrational or impossible parts—audiences infer causal links and will reject wholly irrational sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical classification and use of newly-coined/altered words
rubrics_metrics.description: A newly-coined word is one which has never been even in local use, but is adopted by the poet himself. A word is lengthened when its vowel is exchanged for a longer one or a syllable is inserted; contracted when some part is removed; altered when part of ordinary form is left unchanged and part re-cast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New coinages or altered forms can be employed for effect, distinction, or to fit metre; provide such forms sparingly and where the effect is intelligible. Examples in the text include épviryes for 'sprouters' and other specific forms; these devices are licit when they serve diction and do not obscure sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence can be unified without verb (syntactic allowance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence or phrase may form a unity even if it dispenses with the verb (e.g., 'in walking' or 'Cleon son of Cleon').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing poetic lines, don't require a full clause with verb to achieve unity—elliptical or nominal phrases can function as self-contained meaningful units if they collectively signify one thing or are linked.
